clinicalPearls: Feline oesophagus refers to the endoscopic or radiographic appearance of transient, fine, concentric circular ridges spanning the oesophageal body, resembling the normal oesophagus of a cat.
The rings are produced by transient contraction of the muscularis mucosae and are typically fleeting, appearing and disappearing during endoscopy or on barium swallow.
It is strongly associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and, importantly, with eosinophilic oesophagitis, and can be seen at the moment of reflux or during belching.
Feline oesophagus should be distinguished from the fixed, persistent concentric rings of eosinophilic oesophagitis (trachealisation or a ringed oesophagus), which do not disappear.
The finding itself is benign and transient, but its recognition should prompt evaluation for underlying reflux or eosinophilic oesophagitis when the clinical context fits.
Because the rings are dynamic, they are easily missed or over-called; correlating with symptoms and taking mucosal biopsies helps clarify the significance.
Distal oesophageal biopsies are warranted when dysphagia or food impaction accompanies the appearance, to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis.
No specific treatment is directed at the feline pattern itself; management targets the underlying reflux or eosinophilic disease if present.
reference.pathophysiology: The feline oesophagus pattern arises from transient contraction of the longitudinally oriented muscularis mucosae of the oesophageal body, throwing the mucosa into fine, closely spaced, transverse concentric folds. These contractions are frequently triggered by gastro-oesophageal reflux events, oesophageal distension or belching, which is why the appearance is dynamic and disappears once the stimulus resolves. The phenomenon reflects heightened or reflex mucosal muscle activity rather than fixed structural remodelling. It is distinguished pathophysiologically from the fixed concentric rings of eosinophilic oesophagitis, in which chronic eosinophilic inflammation drives subepithelial fibrosis and lamina propria remodelling, producing persistent rings and a narrow-calibre oesophagus. Recognition of the transient feline pattern therefore serves mainly as a clue to underlying acid reflux or eosinophilic mucosal disease.
additionalDifferentials: eosinophilic oesophagitis with fixed concentric rings (ringed oesophagus)
diffuse oesophageal spasm producing a corkscrew appearance
normal transient contraction waves on imaging
additionalInvestigations: upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with attention to whether rings are transient or fixed
distal and proximal oesophageal mucosal biopsies to assess for eosinophilic infiltration
barium swallow, which may capture the transient ring pattern
ambulatory pH or impedance monitoring for gastro-oesophageal reflux
high-resolution manometry if a motility disorder is suspected
assessment of atopic history and peripheral eosinophilia where eosinophilic oesophagitis is considered
redFlags: recurrent food bolus impaction suggesting eosinophilic oesophagitis or stricture
progressive dysphagia rather than an incidental transient finding
haematemesis or evidence of mucosal ulceration
persistent fixed rings with a narrow-calibre oesophagus
reference.prognosis: The feline oesophagus pattern is itself benign and transient with an excellent prognosis; overall outcome depends entirely on the underlying condition, particularly whether eosinophilic oesophagitis or significant reflux is present and treated.
pitfalls: Mistaking the transient feline pattern for the fixed rings of eosinophilic oesophagitis, or vice versa.
Failing to biopsy the oesophagus in a patient with dysphagia or food impaction and missing eosinophilic oesophagitis.
Over-interpreting a normal fleeting contraction as pathological.
Not investigating for underlying gastro-oesophageal reflux when the pattern is seen.
Attributing dysphagia to the transient rings themselves rather than to the true cause.

management: Recognise the finding as benign and transient and direct management at the underlying cause rather than the rings themselves
Treat associated gastro-oesophageal reflux with proton pump inhibitor therapy and lifestyle measures such as weight reduction, avoiding late meals and elevating the head of the bed
Obtain distal and proximal oesophageal mucosal biopsies to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis when the clinical context fits
Treat confirmed eosinophilic oesophagitis with proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical corticosteroids and dietary elimination
Use ambulatory pH or impedance monitoring and endoscopic reassessment where reflux is refractory or the diagnosis is uncertain
Refer to gastroenterology for persistent dysphagia, refractory symptoms or fixed rings suggesting established eosinophilic oesophagitis
